System Map

Read together, the five themes are not separate pressures. Three loops connect them. Rules filter the queue (B1): a swelling queue of connection requests prompts rules and fees, which remove speculative requests. Bills bring the backlash (B2): rising bills create political pressure, which produces rules that make large users pay. Reservations lengthen the queue (R1): equipment reservations stretch lead times, which push buyers to reserve earlier still. The gas shock and the winter weather act from outside, on prices and on the spare margin. Arrows that cross a colour are connections no single theme carries.

Who connects		A swelling queue prompts rules and fees, and the rules remove speculative requests, which shrinks the queue.Turning: rules written in four markets

Who pays		Rising household bills create political pressure, the pressure produces rules that make large users pay, and those rules keep costs off household bills.Turning in Europe on gas; priming in the US on power

Equipment		Reservations lengthen equipment queues, longer queues stretch lead times, and longer lead times push buyers to reserve still earlier.Turning: queues and lead times still growing

Hover over a status for its meaning: Turning means every step in the loop has current evidence, so it is running now.

The Scenario Matrix’s horizontal axis asks how loop B1 (rules filter the queue) is run: by fees and prices, or by the state choosing who connects. Its vertical axis asks whether loop B2 (bills bring the backlash) closes, so that large users pay, or stalls, so that households do.

What it means: no organisation can stop the gas shock or the weather, but each can fix part of its costs before loop B2 reaches it, take part in the rules that run loop B1, and turn its equipment reservations into decisions so that loop R1 slows.
